What is Transistor? Transistor is a sci-fi themed action RPG that invites players to wield an extraordinary weapon of unknown origin as they fight through a stunning futuristic city.
The game seamlessly integrates thoughtful strategic planning into a fast-paced action experience, melding responsive gameplay and rich atmospheric storytelling.
During the course of the adventure, players will piece together the Transistor's mysteries as they pursue its former owners. [...]

Transistor is Supergiant Games second game after Bastion, an action RPG that sold over 3 million copies.
You play as Red, a famous singer in a city called Cloudbank. On a failed attempt on your life you come in the possesion of the Transistor, a sword-like weapon that the Camerata try to get from you again.

I bought it when it was on Steam Sale and didn't expect much of it, as RPGs are not the genre I normally play.
Yesterday I played straight through it and started the 'recursion' right after that. The artistic value of a game hasn't been so apparent to me for a long time.
Some may argue that in a time of photorealistic CGI, studios with hundreds of incredibly talented artists I must be biased or blind to not recognize their artistic value.
I agree that today there are eye candys everywhere and I am stunned again and again by the realism achieved.
Transistor is something different for me though. It's like a painting with an incredible soundtrack decorated with interactive elements.
While the story kinda flew by me and the game mechanics were cool, the art and soundtrack were what totally mesmerized me..
It resembled an indie version of Remember Me and indie is not meant in a derogative way here, on the contrary.

Transistor is art.
If you look for a straight forward story and hack n slash mechanics, you will be lost.
The vast customizability of your abilities (Functions) and the Turn() mechanic give it strategic depth that imo could be better utilized in form of more challenging fights/bosses or puzzles.
That probably would slow the game down too much and I haven't finished the 'second iteration' so maybe my complaint is unjustified...

 

TL;DR
Action RPG with orgasmic art and music.
Throw money at them so I can enjoy more of their games :)

In the biblical definition, could there be an omniscient, omnipotent being that is both physical and meta-physical at the same time, and is eternal? Explain your logic.
[Discussion] Could there reasonably be a god?

If you truly wish to know, you must look through really thick discourses and dissertations. You will not find such arguments and logic in the space of a Voat comment, it is simply too much of a task. I would recommend looking at Descartes' work, and Thomas Aquinas', for a Christian view of such a God. I sadly cannot recommend other authors for other religion.

I am personally of the conviction that although we can't know if there's a god or not, it is highly unlikely.

One argument that is often put forward against the Christian God is that his omni- attributes are contradictory; so if he knows that something terrible will happen and that he has the power to stop it, why doesn't he? This leads to the conclusion that God either: doesn't care enough to stop said terrible event, doesn't know that the event will happen, or isn't powerful enough to stop it. All three conclusion tend to make people think he isn't worthy of worship.

That seems logical, but you must also entertain the possibility that there is a god. While it may seem possible and logical that there isn't one,nuts also somewhat possible there is one.

How about a god in a more modern sense? Perhaps not all knowing or all powerful, but perhaps a god that created this planet? Or perhaps a being that created this planet that we perceive as god?

there are so many elementary responses to the alleged contradictions in the omni-attributes. i'll just name a few to scratch the surface and hopefully let the conversation grow from there...

  1. in a spacial temporal universe that spans millions of light years in both time and space, our infantile concept of "something terrible" evidences a supreme egotism, without any appreciation for how insignificant anything affecting "me" really is. by way of (extreme) example, we don't know how many hitlers and stalins may have been killed prior to committing bad acts. in the objective world view, we cannot judge any event as terrible because we have limited knowledge of the universe and are handicapped by our subjective perspectives. this is the 'we don't know g-d's plan defense'.
  2. Similar to no.1 but without the positive spin, the alleged "terrible events" aren't important enough for divine intervention. Take 9/11 for example: 3,000 people died. likely more than 100,000 people negatively affected before any wars were fought. several millions affected after. in the span of the world from the beginning of time until the end, it is a mere blip.
  3. if the greatest possible world for mankind is one with free will, divine intervention has to be kept in check, regardless of the consequences, permitting for the extreme examples.
  4. the greatest gift a Creator could have given us is an order to the universe. all technology, day-to-day safety, math, farming, space exploration, etc. is possible only because of the order that underlines the universe. that g-d is unable or unwilling to undo that certainty is evidence of his omni-benevolence and his omnipotence. we would be severely hampered by a greek, olympus-esque situation where the laws of nature were subject to the whims of the almighty.
  5. last: g-d's inability to intervene is part of his greatness, not a criticism. the classic is: what happens if you have a basketball player that could never miss a 3 point shot. throws the ball in the opposite direction, it still goes in. kicks it off the side of his foot? still nothing but net. this guy just cannot miss. would we say that because he cannot miss, that is not the best 3 point shooter? or would we say that because he cannot miss, he is a perfect 3 point shooter. same thing with a creator that cannot limit himself spacially or temporally: his perfection does not allow him these limitations; or better yet, these limitations are inherent to his perfection.

If so, then god is undetectable. I can only use what humans have done throughout history:

1 Saw something unexplainable.

2 Try to explain it.

3 Can't explain it.

4 Attribute to god.

5 Write a lot of stories about it.

6 Re examined and explain it.

but in the meantime, other unexplained stuff gets loaded into item 1. The only way this cycle ends is when all of it is explained. Since it seems to me science creates more questions with each answer, humans are not halfway done.

g-d cannot be limited by spacial or temporal constructs. so he is and always will be metaphysical. kant struggled with this and reconciled it in the prolegomena to any metaphysics when he posited the theory of transcendental idealism (much more complex and instructive than this one-liner, but worth investigating for anyone interested in the physical / metaphysical relationship).

He's murdered many political opponents, sent countless more to be starved and worked to death in forced labor camps, and has consolidated his power in Russia in a way that would make Stalin proud. The economy he oversees functions as well as most economies do under high-level patronage and corruption, even though it would certainly function far better as a market economy with open ties to other markets.

In many ways, Putin is like Russia's Nixon without the checks on his power.

Ultimately, I think Russia will probably remember him with mixed feelings. He did, and is, bringing Russia back from the brink of collapse under low level corruption, and he's replaced the foundering democracy that existed after the Soviet Union's collapse with a functioning plutocracy. When Putin dies or retires, it'll be interesting to see whether Russia steps back from fascism or marches onward down the abyss.
